speaker: dvm
text: Hi, come on in. I'm Doctor Laurent. And this must be Mochi. What's been going on with her?

speaker: client
text: Hi. So she started throwing up on Monday, and it's Thursday now. It's been at least once a day, sometimes twice.

speaker: dvm
text: Okay. Three days of vomiting. What does it look like? Is it food, liquid, hair?

speaker: client
text: The first couple of times it was her food, mostly undigested. Since yesterday it's more like yellow foam, a bit of liquid.

speaker: dvm
text: And is she still eating?

speaker: client
text: Barely. She'll lick the gravy off her wet food and walk away. She's usually a really good eater, so that's what worried me.

speaker: dvm
text: Has she been drinking normally? Any changes in the litter box, like diarrhea, constipation, or bigger clumps of urine?

speaker: client
text: Her stool was a bit soft on Tuesday, but otherwise the same. I haven't noticed her drinking more. If anything, maybe less.

speaker: dvm
text: Is she hiding, or less active than usual?

speaker: client
text: Yeah, she's been sleeping under the bed, which she never does.

speaker: dvm
text: Okay. Any chance she got into something? Plants, string, hair ties, anything like that? Has she been outside?

speaker: client
text: She's indoor only. She does play with hair ties, and I found one chewed up last week. I don't know if she swallowed any of it.

speaker: dvm
text: That's good to know, thank you. Any changes to her food, or anything new in the house?

speaker: client
text: No, same food for years. The salmon pate.

speaker: dvm
text: Is she on any medications or supplements?

speaker: client
text: Just a fish oil supplement in her food. Nothing else.

speaker: dvm
text: And she's nine now, is that right? Spayed?

speaker: client
text: Yes, nine in June, and yes, she's spayed.

speaker: dvm
text: Alright. Let's weigh her first. She's four point one kilos today. In March she was four point six, so she's lost about half a kilo, which is more than ten percent of her body weight for a cat her size.

speaker: client
text: Oh no, I had no idea.

speaker: dvm
text: That's not something you'd see at home. Let me examine her now. Her temperature is thirty-nine point one, which is the upper end of normal. Heart rate is two hundred, and respiratory rate is thirty-two.

speaker: dvm
text: Her gums are pink but a little tacky, and her capillary refill time is under two seconds. Her skin tent is a bit slow, so I'd estimate she's about six percent dehydrated.

speaker: dvm
text: I'd put her body condition at four out of nine. She's lost some muscle over her back and hips.

speaker: dvm
text: Listening to her heart, I don't hear a murmur, and her lungs sound clear. I can't feel an enlarged thyroid gland, but at her age we still want to check her thyroid level.

speaker: dvm
text: On her belly, she's tense and a bit uncomfortable when I press up front, just behind her ribs. I'd call that mild discomfort, a pain score of one out of four. I don't feel any obvious mass or any thickened intestines, and her bladder is a normal size.

speaker: client
text: Is that bad? The discomfort?

speaker: dvm
text: It tells us something is irritated. There are a few possibilities. The most common would be gastritis or dietary upset. Given the hair ties, I am worried about a foreign body, like a piece of string or elastic in her intestines. In a nine year old cat with weight loss, I also want to rule out pancreatitis, kidney disease, hyperthyroidism, and inflammatory bowel disease or intestinal lymphoma.

speaker: client
text: Okay. What would you recommend?

speaker: dvm
text: I'd recommend bloodwork today: a complete blood count, a chemistry panel with electrolytes, and a thyroid level, plus a urinalysis. I'd also really like abdominal x-rays to look for a foreign body.

speaker: client
text: How much would all of that be? Money's a bit tight this month.

speaker: dvm
text: Understood. The bloodwork and urinalysis together are about three hundred and twenty dollars, and the x-rays would add about two hundred and fifty.

speaker: client
text: Can we do the bloodwork today and hold off on the x-rays?

speaker: dvm
text: We can. I'll note that we discussed the x-rays and that you'd like to wait. If she vomits more than twice in a day, stops eating completely, or seems painful, the x-rays become much more important, and you should bring her straight back.

speaker: client
text: That makes sense.

speaker: dvm
text: For treatment today, I'll give her an anti-nausea injection, maropitant, at one milligram per kilo under the skin. I'll also give her one hundred milliliters of lactated Ringer's fluids under the skin to help with the dehydration.

speaker: dvm
text: I'm going to send home mirtazapine ointment to help her appetite. You put a one and a half inch line on the inside of her ear flap once a day, for up to fourteen days. Wear gloves when you apply it.

speaker: client
text: Okay, inside the ear, once a day.

speaker: dvm
text: Exactly. For food, switch to a bland gastrointestinal diet. We'll send you home with the prescription wet food. Feed small amounts, about a tablespoon, every three to four hours to start.

speaker: dvm
text: Please don't give her the fish oil until her stomach settles. And put away anything she could chew, like hair ties and string.

speaker: client
text: I'll do that tonight.

speaker: dvm
text: I'll call you tomorrow afternoon with the bloodwork results. I want to recheck her in three days, on Sunday, or sooner if she gets worse.

speaker: dvm
text: If she vomits more than twice in a day, stops eating entirely, strains in the litter box, or seems weak or painful, come back right away, or go to the emergency hospital if we're closed.

speaker: client
text: Okay. Thank you, Doctor Laurent. I feel better having a plan.

speaker: dvm
text: Of course. The technician will draw her blood now, and then we'll give the injection and the fluids.
